sections.h2: What should a seller know first about Henderson, KY?
sections.html:
Henderson sits on a bluff above the Ohio River in north-central Henderson County, about 10 miles south of Evansville, Indiana, and 30 miles west of Owensboro. The Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate is 27,822 residents, slightly under the 2020 count of 27,981. That slow drift matters to a seller: buyers here are mostly local households, plus commuters who work across the river.

The city is the county seat, so deeds, tax bills and court filings all route through the same downtown blocks. A house with a clean title and no open city orders can close in a few weeks. A house with unpaid weed liens, an estate that has not been probated or a back tax bill takes longer, and those are the files worth sorting out first.

sections.h2: What do the Census numbers say about Henderson homes?
sections.html:
QuickFacts lists the 2020 to 2024 median value of an owner-occupied Henderson home at $160,100, with monthly owner costs of $1,253 for those who carry a mortgage and $494 for those who do not. Median gross rent is $771. About 54.1% of households own their home, which leaves close to half the housing stock in rental hands.

  • Median household income: $48,186, with 18.7% of residents below the poverty line.
  • Households: 12,341, averaging 2.18 people each.
  • Residents 65 and older: 18.8%, a group that often sells an inherited or long-held house.
  • Average commute: 19.8 minutes, short enough that most buyers stay inside the county.

A lower price base means repair costs weigh heavily. A $20,000 roof and furnace job is a large slice of a $160,000 house, which is why many Henderson owners with deferred maintenance choose to sell as-is instead of funding the work first.

sections.h2: How did Henderson's history shape its neighborhoods?
sections.html:
The town began as a river landing called Red Banks, named for the reddish clay bluffs. Its founders laid out the plan in 1797 with unusually wide streets, reportedly to stop a fire from jumping between blocks. Those wide downtown streets still carry diagonal parking and delivery trucks in the center lane. The city was incorporated in January 1840.

Dark tobacco built the town's fortunes in the 1800s, and the warehouses and stemmeries that filled downtown closed over the following century; the last tobacco facility on Pennell Street shut in 1984. Older residential areas such as Audubon, Weaverton and the former East End grew up around that industry, so many houses there date from the early 1900s. If you own one, expect a buyer's inspector to look hard at wiring, plumbing and foundations.

Weather is part of the record too. The Ohio River flood of 1937 spared the bluff, and a local publisher summed it up as a town on the river but never in it. Henderson's climate is humid subtropical, with hot, humid summers and mild to cool winters, so roof age, attic ventilation and air conditioning are routine inspection items.

sections.h2: Which schools, roads and employers draw buyers to Henderson?
sections.html:
Public schools run through the Henderson County school system, which includes eight elementary schools, North Middle and South Middle, and Henderson County High School. Henderson Community College sits in the city, and a Murray State University satellite campus serves adult students. Holy Name of Jesus Catholic School covers elementary and middle grades.

  • US 41 crosses the Bi-State Vietnam Gold Star Bridges to Evansville and runs south toward Madisonville and Hopkinsville.
  • I-69 in Kentucky ends at the US 41 and US 60 interchange at Henderson.
  • Henderson Area Rapid Transit has run public bus service since 1957.
  • Local industry includes aluminum, automotive and appliance parts, plastic injection molding, tool and die work and food processing.

Buyers with jobs at those employers or across the river in Evansville tend to shop within a short drive of US 41.

sections.h2: Who do I call in Henderson before listing or closing?
sections.html:
Most of the paperwork for a sale lands with four offices. The table lists what each one handles.

Henderson offices that touch a sale. Sources: City of Henderson Code Enforcement and Zoning pages; Henderson County FAQ on tax collection.
OfficeWhat it handlesContact detail
City Code EnforcementBuilding codes, property maintenance, signs, zoning questions100 Fifth Street, (270) 831-1277, weekdays 8:00 to 5:00
Board of Zoning AdjustmentVariances, conditional use permits, appeals of zoning decisionsMeets the second Wednesday monthly except January
Henderson County SheriffCurrent real estate tax billsBills mailed late October or early November, payable from November 1
Henderson County ClerkRecording deeds, delinquent tax bills, lien releases20 N Main Street, second floor, (270) 827-5753

Ask Code Enforcement for a written statement of any open orders on the address before you accept an offer, since a buyer's title company will find them anyway.

sections.h2: What happens if my Henderson house has code violations or city liens?
sections.html:
Since July 1, 2017, Henderson has enforced property maintenance and nuisance rules through a Code Enforcement Board. The city posts its final orders and mails a monthly email notice to registered lienholders. Typical entries on the posted list are weeds, rubbish, clutter and inoperable vehicles.

  • A final order can be appealed within 30 days of issue under KRS 65.8831.
  • A lienholder of record has 45 days from the emailed notice to fix the violation or pay the fines and abatement charges.
  • If nobody acts, the city takes lien priority over earlier liens, except liens for state, county, school and city taxes (KRS 65.8835).

A cash buyer can usually pay these charges from the proceeds, but the amounts need to be known before the closing date. Call Code Enforcement at (270) 831-1277 and ask for the file on your parcel.

sections.h2: How are property tax and the deed transfer tax handled at a Henderson closing?
sections.html:
Henderson County real estate bills come from the Sheriff's Office in late October or early November and are payable starting November 1. A bill turns delinquent on January 1 after its due date. Delinquent bills move to the County Clerk, where they gain interest of 1% per month plus penalties, and the unpaid bill stays as a lien on the property until it is paid in full.

The grantor owes Kentucky's deed transfer tax under KRS 142.050: fifty cents for each $500 of value or fraction of it, collected by the county clerk when the deed is recorded. As an illustration only, a house sold at the Census median of $160,100 would carry a tax of $160.50. Deeds in lieu of foreclosure and transfers made under a foreclosure case are exempt, along with some transfers between parent and child for nominal consideration.

The seller normally pays the share of the current year's bill that covers the months of ownership, and the closing agent usually settles it on the statement. Ask the Sheriff's Office for a payoff figure so the numbers match.

sections.h2: Can I sell a Henderson rental or short-term rental property?
sections.html:
Yes, but zoning governs how a buyer can use it. Henderson handles land use through Appendix A of its Code of Ordinances, and Code Enforcement explains setbacks, allowed uses and parking. In April 2024 the Board of Commissioners took up an ordinance amending that appendix for short-term rental property, which touches several residential, business and riverfront districts. Ask Code Enforcement which rules apply to your parcel before you describe it to a buyer as a short-term rental.

If tenants live in the house, bring the lease and the deposit ledger to the first conversation, since a buyer who wants the house vacant will ask when the lease ends.

sections.h2: What are my options for a fast sale in Henderson?
sections.html:
• List with an agent. Best for a house in decent shape in a neighborhood buyers know, though showings and a buyer's mortgage timeline add weeks.
  • Sell as-is to a cash buyer. Skips repair requests, appraisal and loan approval, and can close on a date you choose.
  • Clear the problem first. Paying a small weed lien or finishing probate sometimes opens the retail market again.

Compare the net figure from each route after transfer tax, tax proration, liens and any repairs, not just the headline number.

faqs.q: How fast can a house sell in Henderson, KY?
faqs.a: A cash sale closes on a date you and the buyer agree on, while a conventional sale adds showings, an appraisal and loan approval. The deed still has to be recorded at the Henderson County Clerk, and any open code order or tax bill needs a payoff first.

faqs.q: Who pays the deed transfer tax in Henderson County?
faqs.a: The seller, as grantor, pays it. Kentucky charges $0.50 per $500 of value under KRS 142.050, and the county clerk collects it when the deed is recorded. Foreclosure transfers and deeds in lieu of foreclosure are exempt.

faqs.q: What if I owe back property tax on my Henderson house?
faqs.a: Back taxes must be paid or settled at closing. Bills unpaid after January 1 go to the County Clerk with 1% monthly interest and penalties, and the unpaid amount is a lien on the property. Ask the Clerk's Office at 20 N Main Street for a current payoff.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Henderson house with open Code Enforcement violations?
faqs.a: Yes. The city can file a lien for unpaid fines and abatement costs, and that lien outranks earlier private liens but not tax liens, so the amount comes out of the proceeds. Call Code Enforcement at (270) 831-1277 for the file before you set a price.

faqs.q: Do I need to make repairs before selling a Henderson home?
faqs.a: No. An as-is sale to a cash buyer does not require repairs, and a retail buyer may ask for them after inspection. With a median owner-occupied value of $160,100, a large repair bill can take a big share of the sale price, so get quotes before deciding.
